title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: tip a candle and the flame still climbs upward, and the Vaisheshika Sutra names the unseen thing behind it

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika finished its list of substances with the self, known by the breath, and the mind, a gate for one thing at a time. Who got your whole attention? Today is our last day with Vaisheshika. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.
screen: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.` · `VAISHESHIKA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: Light a candle and tilt it. The wax leans, the wick leans, and the flame doesn't. It keeps climbing straight up, as if something above it were calling. Step outside, and the wind isn't climbing. It runs sideways across the field. Nobody taught the flame to rise or the wind to run. They just do. A school that explains the world with atoms and categories has to say something about that. Why does anything start moving the way it does? The Vaisheshika Sutra gives an answer in a single line, and the answer is a word that means, simply, unseen.
screen: `TILT THE CANDLE.` → `THE FLAME STILL CLIMBS.` → `WHY DOES ANYTHING MOVE?`

segments.voice: The word is adrishta: the unseen. The Sutra says that fire's flaming upward, wind's blowing sideways, the first movement of the atoms and the first movement of the mind are all caused by adrishta. Not by anything you can point to. By the unseen. So what is it? In this school, the unseen force is bound up with what beings have done. Actions leave something behind, merit and its opposite, and that unseen residue helps shape what happens next, down to how atoms first come together into a world fit for those who will live in it. Atoms, categories, and underneath them, the moral weight of what we do. That's the dharma the Sutra opened with, showing up again at the bottom of physics. Then there's God. Near its opening, the Sutra says the Veda is authoritative because it is the word of That. Commentators read That in different ways. Some read it as God, Ishvara. Others read it as dharma, which the Veda teaches. Later thinkers in the joined Nyaya-Vaisheshika school, Udayana among them, argued at length that the unseen needs a knower to guide it, and that the knower is Ishvara, who sets the atoms moving in keeping with what beings have earned. So within one school you'll find readers who see God in that line and readers who see dharma. Vaisheshika leaves you with this. The world is made of tiny, lasting things, sorted into kinds, each thing particular. And moving through all of it is something you'll never see directly: the weight of what's been done.
screen: `ADRISHTA: THE UNSEEN.` · `FIRE RISES, WIND RUNS SIDEWAYS.` · `WHAT WE DO LEAVES SOMETHING BEHIND.` · `THAT: GOD, OR DHARMA?` · then, large: `THE WEIGHT OF WHAT'S BEEN DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the unseen at work. If you have a candle, light it and watch the flame rise; if not, picture a flame in your mind's eye, or simply watch your breath rise and fall. Settle. Then think of one small thing you did yesterday: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or dropped. You can't see what it left behind. Let it sit there anyway, the way the flame keeps climbing. Don't judge it. Just notice that it's still somewhere, moving things a little. If you pray, you can hold yesterday's actions before Ishvara, or the name of God you use. The bell holds the time.
Vaisheshika. The school of atoms, categories and particulars, where even the first motion of the world runs on adrishta, the unseen left behind by what we do.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Today, do one small thing well that nobody will ever see. Let it go into the unseen. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, adrishta is taught as the unseen result of past actions, and later thinkers such as Udayana argued that Ishvara guides it; students meet these arguments after learning the categories.

original.note: Sanskrit: adrishta, the unseen; in Vaisheshika, the unseen force left by actions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a school of atoms explains everything by matter alone.
what it means: in Vaisheshika, the unseen, adrishta, left behind by what beings do, starts the very first motion of the atoms.
what a scholar hears: Vaisheshika Sutra 5.2.13 credits fire's rising, wind's sideways motion, and the first motion of atoms and mind to adrishta.

notes: Editor pass: trapdoor floor 1 changed; it said a school of atoms has no room for the unseen, which clashed with 1167, where atoms themselves are never seen.
Vaisheshika Sutra 5.2.13 (agner urdhvajvalanam vayos tiryakpavanam anumanasos cadyam karmety adrstakaritani): paraphrased; confirm numbering in the recension used.
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.3 (tadvacanad amnayasya pramanyam): the two readings of 'tad' (Ishvara or dharma) are presented without ranking; confirm the description of the commentarial split.
Adrishta as the unseen residue of merit and demerit that shapes creation: standard; confirm the phrasing 'a world fit for those who will live in it'.
Udayana's Nyayakusumanjali is named without a date; confirm 'argued at length that the unseen needs a knower to guide it' fairly summarizes one of his arguments.
Fork is not graded; the 'answer' is that the school holds both readings.
Last Vaisheshika day; the close points to Samkhya. Tomorrow's title is kept exactly as the index ('Samkhya (the 24 principles', open parenthesis); the close screen adds the closing parenthesis.
